## Overview

The Tonto Apache, who call themselves *Dilzhę́’é*, are a band of Western Apache people in Arizona. Their ancestral territory extended from the San Francisco Peaks, East Verde River, and Oak Creek Canyon along the Verde River into the Mazatzal Mountains, the Salt River, the Tonto Basin, and toward the Little Colorado River. The Tonto Apache Reservation is south of Payson, Arizona, within the Tonto National Forest, and consists of 85 acres. It serves about 100 tribal members of the 140 total; 110 are enrolled tribal members. Other Tonto Apache live among the San Carlos Apache and Fort Apache communities, or belong to the Yavapai-Apache Nation of the Camp Verde Indian Reservation. Their language is the Tonto dialect of Western Apache, a Southern Athabaskan language. Their folk-culture record is closely connected with hunter-gatherer life, bilingual relations with Yavapai communities, rancheria organization, and named local bands.

## Material culture

### Textile & pattern traditions

**Motif vocabulary.** The sources name no textile motifs.

### Clothing & dress

The sources describe differences between Yavapai and Apache clothing. Yavapai moccasins were described as rounded, while Apache moccasins had pointed toes. The sources also state that Yavapai were often tattooed, whereas Apaches seldom had tattoos, and that painted designs on faces differed between the groups. No Tonto Apache garments, head coverings, belts, ceremonial clothing, or dress materials are identified.

### Architecture

The smallest Tonto Apache social unit was the matrilocal and matrilineal family living in one *wickiup*, also called *kowa* or *gowa*. Each wife lived with her children in a separate wickiup. Several related families could live together as an extended family, called a *gotah*, within a rancheria, and several gotah formed local groups. Tonto Apache and Yavapai communities also lived together in common rancherias. At the Yavapai-Apache Reservation near Camp Verde, the Yavapai and Tonto Apache constructed irrigation systems, including a five-mile, or 8 km, ditch.

### Ceramics, metalwork & everyday objects

 They mention hunting and gathering equipment only generally, and state that the Tonto Apache lacked many European goods that Navajo sheep raising enabled the Navajo to obtain through trade, including blankets, foods, and various tools.

### Jewelry & body adornment

The sources provide no account of Tonto Apache jewelry, ornaments, hair practices, or ritual adornment. They state only that Yavapai were often tattooed while Apaches seldom had tattoos, and that painted facial designs differed between the two groups.

## Music & performance

 They identify the Tonto dialect as one of the three dialects of the Western Apache language and describe bilingual Tonto Apache–Yavapai communities in which people spoke both the Tonto dialect and Yavapai. The sources also state that band headmen commonly had two names, one from each linguistic tradition.

## Dance & theatre

 They mention funeral practices as one feature that differed between Yavapai and Apache peoples, without describing those practices.

## Festivals & rituals

 They state that funeral practices differed between Yavapai and Apache peoples. Historically, when food stocks were running low, a respected woman, described as a “woman chief” or elder, publicly called attention to the situation and asked rancheria leaders to organize raids to obtain needed supplies. This was part of the social and subsistence system rather than a named festival.

The sources describe warfare, raiding, and common defense as important reasons for band organization. The highest social unit was the group or band, usually composed of several local groups, and it was organized mostly for military purposes and common defense. The Tonto Apache and neighboring Yavapai also raided and warred together against enemy peoples such as the Tohono O'odham and the Akimel O'odham.

## Foodways

The Tonto Apache were typically hunter-gatherers. They hunted antelope, deer, birds, bush rats, and other game, and gathered wild agave, berries, wild plants, and seeds. Women also cultivated watermelons, pumpkins, corn, later grain, and other crops. Some Northern Tonto groups depended entirely on hunting and gathering wild plant foods because they were exposed to hostile Navajo communities to the north and east.

The Yavapai and Tonto Apache at the Camp Verde Reservation constructed irrigation systems that enabled sufficient harvests and made the community relatively self-sufficient. The sources describe an irrigation ditch five miles, or 8 km, long. On Fossil Creek, one Tonto Apache band hunted and gathered and maintained a few tiny farms. No named Tonto Apache dishes, cooking methods, beverages, food taboos, ceremonial foods, or preservation techniques are recorded.

## Oral tradition & literature

 They preserve a vocabulary of personal, place, band, and group names in Apache and Yavapai, including *Dilzhę́’é*, the Western Apache name used by the Tonto Apache and also by the San Carlos Apache. The sources state that the etymology of Dilzhę́’é is unclear, although it may translate as “people with high-pitched voices.”

The sources also record names associated with local groups and bands. Examples include *Dasziné Dasdaayé Indee*, “Porcupine Sitting Above People”; *Tsé Hichii Indee*, “Horizontal Red Rock People”; *Tú Dotłʼizh Indee*, “Blue Water People”; *Dotłʼizhi HaʼitʼIndee*, “Turquoise Road Coming Up People”; and *Tsé Nołtłʼizhn*, “Rocks in a Line of Greenness People.” No contemporary literary revival or preservation project is described.

## Language & religion

The Tonto Apache speak the Tonto dialect of the Western Apache language, which belongs to the Southern Athabaskan language family. The Tonto dialect is one of three Western Apache dialects and is described as the most distinct from the other two Apache dialects, possibly because of the close connection with Yavapai communities. The Apache name for the language is given as *Ndee biyati' / Nnee biyati'*. Yavapai belongs to the Upland Yuman branch.

Tonto Apache and Yavapai people often lived together in bilingual mixed-tribal bands. People commonly spoke both languages, and headmen usually had two names, one Apache and one Yavapai.
